# Turning anomalies into warnings: the tuning run

*Generated by `npm run tune:warning`. Do not edit by hand.*

Run 2026-09-13T18:14:01.795Z over a 128-district panel drawn from all 36 states and union territories (of 769 modelled districts; see the panel note in the script), 3 independent rounds of 42 injected surges each (126 surges, 258 clean district-observations).

## What is being asked

The detector flags POINTS. At `AI.DETECT_ANOMALIES`' own 0.95 threshold over 28 scored days, roughly 1.4 flagged points per series are expected by chance, so most districts have one and a
product that treated a point as a warning would raise one in most districts. A warning is therefore a RULE:

> **k** consecutive days flagged high, each at least **e** above the model's own upper bound.

Surges are injected into the real series -- 14 days, 4-day ramp, multipliers 1.5/2/3, on three epidemiological patterns -- and the real detector is run over the result. The detector never sees which districts were touched.

## The dilution, which decides everything below

An outbreak doubles the caseload of ONE disease. The drugs that treat it double with it. Total OPD does not:

| Pattern | Share of a district's OPD | A 2x outbreak arrives in footfall as |
|---|---|---|
| `monsoon_vector` | 9% | x1.09 |
| `summer_enteric` | 7% | x1.07 |
| `winter_respiratory` | 9% | x1.09 |

So the two series are not two views of one signal at different lags. They have different sensitivity, and
the table below measures both rather than assuming the upstream one wins because it is upstream.

## The table

Detection is at the gate's 2x scenario. Lead time is the gap between the warning and the first affected shelf
in that district emptying under the surged rate. A false alarm is a warning in a district where nothing was
injected, or one that fired outside the surge window in a district where something was.

Gate: detection at 2x >= 80%, median lead >= 4 days, false alarms <= 0.5 per district-week.

## The rule the product uses

**k=2, e=0.1, on the `consumption` series.**

| | |
|---|---|
| Detection rate, 2x 14-day surge | 100% (36 of 36) |
| Median lead time before the first shelf empties | 4.6 d (n=121) |
| False alarms per district-week | 0.446 (460 over 1032 clean district-weeks) |
| Precision | 21% |

Detection by surge size, same rule:

| Multiplier | Surges | Detected | Rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| x1.5 | 42 | 39 | 93% |
| x2 | 36 | 36 | 100% |
| x3 | 48 | 48 | 100% |

Chosen from the 2 rules that clear the gate, by PRECISION
-- but it is worth stating what the criterion is, because the wrong one is the easy one. Detection can always be
bought by lowering the bar, so detection rate is not it. The lowest false-alarm rate is not it either: that was
the first version of this choice, and it selected a rule whose warnings were wrong four times in five. Precision
is what decides whether the fifth alert gets opened, so precision is optimised subject to the gate.

**21% precision is not a good number, and it is the honest one.** The gate this project set itself -- from the design note, before any of this was measured -- constrains
detection, lead time and the false alarm rate, and says nothing about precision.
On this evidence it should have: the tighter rules k=3 e=0.1 and k=3 e=0 reach 53% and 42% precision for 83% and 86% detection, and miss the gate only on the 4-day lead.
Moving the gate now, after seeing the table, would turn every number on this page into an argument. It is recorded here instead.

## Precision is reported at an unrealistically favourable base rate

In each round 42 of 128 districts (33%) are having an outbreak. Real outbreak prevalence is far lower, and precision falls with the base rate
however good the detector is -- so the precision column here is an upper bound on what a district would see.

**False alarms per district-week is the number that does not move with the base rate**, which is exactly why the
design note asks for it. At the chosen rule it is the rate a single district experiences: one spurious warning
every 2 weeks.

## What this does not measure

- **The demand is simulated.** The surge is injected into a series this project generated, so the detector is
  being tested on data whose noise structure it did not have to discover. Real HMIS OPD returns carry reporting
  artefacts -- late entry, batch backfill, camp days -- that no simulation here reproduces.
- **Consumption is censored by stock and footfall is not.** A district already out of the relevant drug cannot
  show rising consumption however large the outbreak, which is exactly when a warning matters most.
- **Shelves that were going to empty anyway are excluded from the lead time.** Across the 126 scenarios, 1,587 affected positions had less than 14 days of cover at their NORMAL rate, so no outbreak warning could have saved them; 5,042 had enough cover for the surge to be the difference, and those are the ones the lead is measured on.
- **Lead time assumes the surged rate continues.** The shelf-emptying day is `onHand / (m x daily demand)`
  over the district's simulated positions; a resupply arriving mid-surge would extend it.
